meta.title: Scripture-Based Prayer Prompts: 12 Verses to Pray From
meta.description: Scripture-based prayer prompts for praise, thanks, confession, requests and intercession: 12 KJV verses, a three-question method and a lock-screen setup.

sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: FaithWall is the easiest way to keep scripture-based prayer prompts where you'll actually use them: you choose the verses, and it puts them on your iPhone lock screen as a wallpaper or as a widget that rotates on its own. The 12 prompts below each pair one verse with one question. The verse gives you the words, and the question tells you where to take them.

sections.text: **Scripture-based prayer prompts** fix the most common way prayer stalls. You sit down, you mean it, and the only thing that comes out is the list of what's worrying you. A prompt is a verse plus one question that turns it back toward God. Write them in a notebook and they wait for you to remember the notebook. Put them on your lock screen with FaithWall and they're waiting on a screen you check anyway.

sections.label: of Protestant churchgoers read the Bible or a devotional during their time alone with God
sections.description: Per Lifeway Research's survey of 1,002 U.S. Protestant churchgoers. In the same survey, 83% said they pray in their own words.

sections.text: That gap is why prompts work. For most people, prayer happens every day and Scripture happens on some other day, as two separate habits. A short set of **Scripture-based prayer prompts** joins them in under a minute: one verse, one question, and your prayer starts in God's words instead of your to-do list. For the wider setup (reminders, widgets, routines), the [prayer life on iPhone hub](/prayer-life-iphone) maps the whole picture. If you also want a dedicated prayer app, start with [our best prayer app for iPhone picks](/blog/best-prayer-app-for-iphone).
How do you turn a Bible verse into a prayer prompt?

Ask the verse three questions, in this order: what does it show me about God, what does it ask of me, and who else needs it? The first question leads to praise or thanks, the second to confession or a request, and the third to intercession. It works on almost any verse, including one you didn't pick for prayer.

items: **What does this show me about God?** Praise him for exactly that. Skip the general "you're good" and name the specific thing this verse says he is or does.
**What does it ask of me?** Confess where you've fallen short of it, or ask for help to live it today.
**Who else needs it?** Name one person and pray the verse over them by name.

sections.text: Put your prompts on the lock screen in one setup

Save the verses you want to pray from in FaithWall, then show them as a full-screen wallpaper or as a lock-screen widget. For prompts, the widget is the better fit. It rotates through your saved verses on a timer, so each glance at your phone can bring a different starting point without you changing anything.

items: Download **FaithWall** from the App Store. It's free to download, a subscription unlocks it, and the App Store shows the price before you pay.
Search or browse to the verses below, or your own, and save them. You choose every verse, in any of 24 translations.
Pick the lock-screen widget and set it to rotate every hour, every 8 hours or once a day.
Press and hold your lock screen, tap **Customize**, choose the lock screen, then tap the widget row under the clock and pick the app's widget.

sections.content: **Karol's call, as the developer:** set the rotation to every 8 hours. That gives you three prompts a day, roughly morning, midday and evening, which is the rhythm David describes below. Hourly moves too fast to actually pray what you see, and once a day lets a verse go stale by lunch.

sections.text: Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.

sections.content: **A list of prompts in your Notes app waits for you to remember it. A prompt on your lock screen is already there when you pick up your phone,** which you'll do many times today for reasons that have nothing to do with prayer. Being in sight is the one thing a prompt needs before it gets prayed.

sections.text: 12 Scripture-based prayer prompts, grouped by how you pray

These follow the movements most churchgoers already use. Lifeway's same survey found that 80% thank God and 62% praise him during their time alone with him, while 49% confess sins. Each prompt below is one KJV verse and one line to pray from it. Save the verses and keep the lines in your head.
Praise

items: Psalm 145:3: "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised." Name one way God has been bigger than the problem you woke up with.
Lamentations 3:22–23: "His compassions fail not. They are new every morning." What mercy is here this morning that wasn't here yesterday? Say it out loud.

sections.text: Thanksgiving

items: Psalm 103:2: "Forget not all his benefits." Name three from the last 24 hours, specifically. "The call with my sister" counts for more than "my family."
1 Thessalonians 5:18: "In every thing give thanks." Find one thing to thank God for inside the situation you'd rather not be in.

sections.text: Confession

items: Psalm 139:23: "Search me, O God, and know my heart." Ask him to show you one thing from today, then wait before you move on.
1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us." Name it specifically. "Everything" isn't a confession.

sections.text: Asking

items: Philippians 4:6: "In every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving." Turn today's worry into a one-sentence request, then attach one thank-you to it.
James 1:5: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God." Name the decision in front of you and ask about that one, not about life in general.

sections.text: Intercession

items: 1 Timothy 2:1: "Intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." Pray by name for one person you haven't thought about in a month.
Matthew 5:44: "Pray for them which despitefully use you." Pray for the person who got under your skin this week, for their good rather than their correction.

sections.text: Listening

items: Psalm 46:10: "Be still, and know that I am God." Stop talking. Give it one full minute of quiet before you say anything else.
1 Samuel 3:10: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." End with Samuel's sentence, and then actually wait.

sections.text: If the Psalms prompts open something up, go further with the Bible's own prayer book. [Praying through the Psalms](/blog/praying-through-the-psalms-app) is a 30-day practice built on the same idea, with the Psalter itself as the prompt list.
Where this gets hard

The prompts aren't the hard part. Keeping them in front of you is. Most people who try **Scripture-based prayer prompts** write them on an index card or in the Notes app, use them for a week, and then the card ends up in a drawer. Rotation dies next. You meant to move to a new verse every few days, and by week two you've looked at the same one so long that your eyes skip it. FaithWall handles both problems. The verses sit on the lock screen instead of behind an app icon, and the widget moves to your next saved verse on its timer, so the prompt changes before you stop seeing it.

sections.content: **The lock screen shows the verse, not the question.** The app displays the verses you saved. It doesn't write prompts or choose verses for you, which is why the three questions above matter: they work on whichever verse comes up.

sections.text: Questions people ask about praying from Scripture
Can I write my own prayer prompts from the Bible?

Yes, and you should once the 12 above feel familiar. Take a verse from whatever you're reading this week and run the three questions on it. If it gives you nothing to praise, confess or ask, pick another. Not every verse makes a good prompt, and that's fine.
How many prompts should I rotate at once?

Start with six to twelve. With fewer than six you'll memorize the rotation within a week. With more than twelve, each verse comes round too rarely to sink in. At an 8-hour rotation, twelve saved verses means each one comes up about every four days.
Should I add a home-screen widget too?

Only if you pray at a desk with your phone in view. The [daily prayer widget guide](/blog/daily-prayer-widget-ios) walks through widget placement on both screens. Start with the lock screen, because you see it every time you pick up your phone, including the times you didn't mean to.
